title: Orlistat | NHS inform
text:
Orlistat
Orlistat works by preventing around a third of the fat from the food you eat being absorbed. The undigested fat isn’t absorbed into your body. It’s passed out with your poo. This will help you avoid gaining weight, but won’t necessarily cause you to lose weight.
You can only use orlistat if a healthcare professional thinks it’s the right medicine for you. In most cases, orlistat is only available on prescription. Only one product (Alli) is available over the counter directly from pharmacies, under the supervision of a pharmacist.
Before starting to take orlistat, you should:
speak to your healthcare professional about whether its right for you
start eating a
balanced diet
increase the amount of
exercise you are currently doing
You should keep eating a balanced diet and exercising during your treatment. You should also continue this after you stop taking orlistat.
When orlistat should be used
You’ll only be recommended to take orlistat if you’ve attempted to lose weight through:
diet
exercise
lifestyle changes
You’ll also need to have:
a
body mass index (BMI)
of 28 or more, and other weight-related conditions, like high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes
a BMI of 30 or more
Your doctor will talk to you about the benefits of taking orlistat. They’ll also talk to you about the potential side effects.
Orlistat isn’t usually recommended for people who are pregnant or breastfeeding.
Dosage and duration of treatment
You should take 1 orlistat capsule with water with each main meal. You should take it either immediately before, during or one hour after each main meal.
If you miss a meal, or the meal doesn’t contain any fat, you shouldn’t need to take the orlistat capsule. Your healthcare professional should explain this to you. You can also check the patient information leaflet that comes with your medicine.
Your treatment should only go beyond 3 months if you’ve lost 5% of your body weight. It usually starts to affect how you digest fat within one to two days.
Once you’ve achieved your agreed target weight, talk to your healthcare professional about stopping treatment.
Speak to your healthcare professional if you haven’t lost weight after 3 months.
Taking orlistat with other health conditions
Talk to your healthcare professional before starting orlistat if you have another serious health condition like:
type 2 diabetes
high blood pressure
kidney disease
It may be necessary to change the dose of your medicine.
If you have type 2 diabetes, it may take you longer to lose weight using orlistat. Your target weight loss after three months may therefore be slightly lower.
Side effects
Common side effects of orlistat include:
fatty or oily poo
needing the toilet urgently
pooing more frequently
severe
diarrhoea
an oily discharge from your anus (you may have oily spots on your underwear)
flatulence (wind)
stomach pain
headaches
These side effects are much less likely to occur if you stick to a low-fat diet.
Orlistat may cause severe
diarrhoea
. If you’re taking the combined pill, you should use additional
contraception
, like
condoms
. This is because the contraceptive pill may not be absorbed by your body if you have diarrhoea. This could make it less effective.
Reporting side effects
You can report any side effect or adverse reaction to orlistat using the
Yellow Card Scheme
. This can help the Medicines & Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) identify new side effects or risks associated with medicines.
Include as much detail as possible, particularly any brand name or manufacturer’s details.
